The Life's Work, Teaching and Legacy of Rabbi Shlomo Adani, Author of "Melekhet Shlomo"
The literature of Mishnah commentary underwent a historical and methodological turning point in the transition between the 16th and 17th centuries, a period in which the foundations were laid for textual criticism and for precise textual interpretation of the Oral Torah [cite: 1, 2, 3]. At the center of this scholarly flourishing stands the unique figure of Rabbi Shlomo ben Yeshua Adani (5337–5385 approximately / 1567–1625), a Talmudic scholar who was born in Yemen, grew up in conditions of poverty and distress in Safed and Jerusalem, and was active for most of his life in the city of Hebron [cite: 1, 4, 5]. His great work, the "Melekhet Shlomo" commentary on the six orders of the Mishnah, constitutes one of the towering interpretive achievements in the history of rabbinic literature [cite: 1, 4]. The importance of the work is measured not only by the extent of the author's Talmudic and halakhic mastery, but first and foremost by his critical-textual method, unprecedented for its time [cite: 1, 2, 3]. While the sages of Europe relied mainly on common printed editions, Adani exploited his location in the Land of Israel to compare dozens of ancient manuscripts, rare Eastern versions, glosses of the sages of Safed, and even the original manuscript of the Rambam [cite: 6, 7, 8].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life, His Period and His Living Conditions
The life story of Rabbi Shlomo Adani is marked by severe personal tragedies and constant material distress, which magnify the tremendous achievement of writing his comprehensive work [cite: 1, 5, 9, 10]. He was born in 5327 (1567) in the city of Sana'a in Yemen [cite: 1]. His father, Mari Yeshua ben David ben Chalfon Adani, was a prominent Torah scholar from Sana'a who supported his family in great austerity as a grocer [cite: 1]. When Shlomo was only four years old, in 5331 (1571), the family decided to immigrate to the Land of Israel and settled in Safed, which was at that time a flourishing spiritual, kabbalistic and halakhic center [cite: 1, 5].
The family's stay in Safed was marked by heavy disasters following the plagues and famine that struck the region [cite: 1, 9]. Rabbi Shlomo's mother and brother died one after the other, and the impoverished family moved to Jerusalem [cite: 1, 5, 9]. Disaster continued to pursue Rabbi Shlomo, and in 5342 (1582), when he was only fifteen years old, his father also died and he was left a complete orphan, solitary and abandoned [cite: 1, 5]. In his moving introduction to his commentary "Melekhet Shlomo," the author reveals with rare candor his physical and emotional suffering in those days [cite: 1, 5, 10]. For about two and a half years he lived in the streets of Jerusalem, sleeping on garbage heaps and in ruins, and suffering the disgrace of hunger [cite: 1, 5, 9]. Out of shame and poverty, he used to flee on Sabbath nights to the fields surrounding the city so as not to be seen by members of the community leaving the synagogues [cite: 1, 9].
The turning point in his life occurred when the wealthy rabbi R. Moshe Chami, an affluent Torah scholar who had come from Egypt to Jerusalem, noticed the boy's diligence and prominent talents and took him into his home [cite: 1, 5, 9]. R. Moshe Chami provided for all of Rabbi Shlomo's needs for seven years, enabled him to devote all his time to in-depth Torah study, and even arranged his marriage in 5340 (1589) [cite: 1, 5].
After his marriage Rabbi Shlomo Adani moved to live in Hebron, where a small and poor Jewish community lived under Ottoman rule [cite: 1, 7]. In Hebron he made his home until the day of his death, but there too he suffered heavy disasters [cite: 1, 5]. All his children who were born to him in Hebron (seven or eleven according to different sources) died in their youth from plagues and severe illnesses, afterward his wife also died, and he was again left solitary, ill and childless [cite: 1, 5]. Unlike the prevailing custom among the sages of Yemen of earning a living from manual labor, Rabbi Shlomo Adani did not engage in trade in Hebron and made a meager living as a teacher of young children and as a person supported by others [cite: 1, 9]. Out of bereavement and a sense of the transience of the world, he devoted all his inner resources to writing his commentary on the Mishnah, with the aim of leaving a memorial for future generations [cite: 10].
Stage in His Life | Approximate Date | Description of the Event and Its Historical Context
Birth in Sana'a | 5327 (1567) | Born to Mari Yeshua Adani, one of the sages of Sana'a who made his living from a tiny grocery shop [cite: 1].
Immigration to the Land of Israel | 5331 (1571) | The family immigrated to the Land of Israel at age 4; settled in Safed and suffered the disgrace of hunger and illness [cite: 1, 9].
Move to Jerusalem and orphanhood | 5342 (1582) | His father died in Jerusalem when he was 15, after his mother and brother died in Safed [cite: 1, 5, 9].
Patronage of R. Moshe Chami | 5342–5340 (1582–1589) | Taken in and supported by the benefactor and rabbi R. Moshe Chami for seven years until his marriage [cite: 1, 5].
Move to Hebron and start of writing | 5340 (1589) | Settled in Hebron and began recording glosses on the margins of the Mishnah [cite: 1].
Completion of "Melekhet Shlomo" | 5382–5384 (1622–1624) | Completion of the third and final edition of the commentary in Hebron [cite: 1, 7, 11].
Death in Hebron | approximately 5385 (1625) | His death in Hebron and burial in the ancient cemetery of the city [cite: 4, 5].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Teachers, His Torah Circle and the Circumstances of His Work
The spiritual formation of Rabbi Shlomo Adani took place at the very heart of the Torah center in the Land of Israel in the 16th century [cite: 1, 4]. In Jerusalem he merited to learn from the great men of the generation, who left an indelible mark on his method of work [cite: 1, 4, 5]. His distinguished teacher was Rabbi Betzalel Ashkenazi, author of the book "Shitah Mekubbetzet" and one of the greatest decisors in Egypt and the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 4]. From Rabbi Betzalel, Adani adopted the critical-interpretive approach, the aspiration to collect different manuscripts, and the practice of recording glosses, versions and explanations in the margins of books [cite: 1]. At the same time, he studied Torah and Kabbalah in Jerusalem from Rabbi Chaim Vital, the distinguished student of the Ari, and also studied with Rabbi Shlomo Amirillo and other sages [cite: 1, 4].
The circumstances of the composition of his commentary "Melekhet Shlomo" are directly connected to the guidance he received from his teachers [cite: 1]. Following the method of Rabbi Betzalel Ashkenazi, Adani used to record in the margins of the Mishnah from which he studied various notes and versions [cite: 1]. While living in Hebron, these glosses were seen by the scholar Rabbi David Amirillo, whom he had known since childhood in Safed [cite: 9, 10]. Rabbi David Amirillo recognized the tremendous value of the notes and warned Adani that if he did not put them into an orderly book, the margins of the Mishnah would wear out and the work would go to waste [cite: 9, 10]. To carry out the plan, R. David Amirillo contributed to Rabbi Shlomo the paper and writing materials, and urged him to gather the study material into a comprehensive work [cite: 1, 9, 10].
During his work in Hebron a fascinating conceptual cross-fertilization occurred between Adani's work and the work of Rabbi Yom Tov Lipmann Heller (author of the "Tosafot Yom Tov") [cite: 9, 10]. While Adani was diligently engaged in his commentary in isolated Hebron, the "Tosafot Yom Tov" composed his commentary in Prague [cite: 9]. When a sage from Europe came to Hebron and brought with him the book "Tosafot Yom Tov," Rabbi Shlomo Adani studied it and was astonished to see how two sages at opposite ends of the world had aimed at the same difficulties, resolutions and versions [cite: 9, 10]. Adani saw in this divine providence, and in the later editions of his work he incorporated many references to the words of the "Tosafot Yom Tov," commenting on them, bringing support for them, or humbly disagreeing with them [cite: 9, 10, 12]. In addition, he was deeply influenced by the glosses of Rabbi Yehosef Ashkenazi ("the Divine Tanna" of Safed), who devoted his life to clarifying the text of the Mishnayot according to ancient manuscripts, and incorporated his glosses as a central component of his commentary [cite: 6, 7].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Torah Writings and the Structure of "Melekhet Shlomo"
Rabbi Shlomo Adani composed several Torah works, but his main fame and life's work rest on his commentary on the Mishnah [cite: 1, 4].
Title of the Work | Field of Engagement | State of the Work and Its Writing | Importance and Characteristics
Melekhet Shlomo | A comprehensive and critical commentary on the six orders of the Mishnah [cite: 1, 4]. | Written between 5340 and 5384 (1589–1624); preserved in autograph [cite: 1, 7]. | Textual clarifications, comparison of manuscripts, grammar and summary of the decisors [cite: 1, 2, 3].
Divrei Emet | Glosses and textual clarifications on Scripture and the Masorah [cite: 1, 4]. | Lost; existed in manuscript and was quoted by the Chida [cite: 1, 4]. | A work in the tradition of the "Or Torah" of Rabbi Menachem de Lonzano and the book "Minchat Shai" [cite: 1, 4].
Binyan Shlomo | Glosses and novellae on the Order Kodashim in the Babylonian Talmud [cite: 1]. | Partly preserved in manuscripts [cite: 1]. | Clarification of topics in the Order Kodashim and in the commentary of Rashi and the Tosafot [cite: 1].
Sela HaMachloket | A comprehensive clarification of disputes among the Rishonim [cite: 7]. | Partly incorporated into the manuscript of "Melekhet Shlomo" [cite: 7]. | Includes the copying of rare commentaries of the Rishonim on the minor tractates [cite: 7].
The work on the "Melekhet Shlomo" commentary spanned about 35 years (from 5340 to 5384 / 1589–1624) and went through three main editions at the author's hand [cite: 1, 7, 11]. The third and final edition was written and completed in Hebron between 5382 and 5384 (1622–1624) [cite: 1, 4, 7, 11]. The original manuscript of the work (the autograph) was written in a tiny, dense Eastern script, and was divided by the author into four volumes [cite: 7]:
* The first volume covers from the Order Zeraim through tractate Yoma [cite: 7].
* The second volume covers from tractate Sukkah through tractate Kiddushin [cite: 7].
* The third volume covers from tractate Bava Kamma through tractate Bekhorot [cite: 7].
* The fourth volume covers from tractate Arakhin through the end of the Order Taharot [cite: 7].
The name of the book, "Melekhet Shlomo," was chosen by the author out of extreme humility [cite: 9, 10]. In his introduction he notes that the work is not the fruit of his "wisdom" but the fruit of his "labor" – the work of collecting, writing, copying and comparing the words of the ancients [cite: 9, 10]. At the same time, he sought to perpetuate his name as a memorial for future generations, since he remained childless, without sons to carry on his name [cite: 10].
The importance of the manuscript extends beyond the field of the Mishnah alone [cite: 7]. In the margins of the commentary Rabbi Shlomo Adani copied entire works of Rishonim that were not available in print at that time, including the commentary of the Rosh, the Ra'avad and Rabbi Zerachia HaLevi (the Razah) on tractate Kinnim, and the introductions of the Rambam and Rabbi Ovadia of Bartenura to the Order Taharot from precisely corrected versions [cite: 7].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Interpretive and Textual Method
The interpretive method of Rabbi Shlomo Adani places him as one of the harbingers of textual-scientific criticism in the interpretation of the Oral Torah [cite: 1, 2, 3]. This bridging between traditional Talmudic scholarship and rigorous textual analysis rests on four central foundations [cite: 1, 2, 6, 8]:
First, Adani placed at the center of his work textual criticism and the comparison of versions [cite: 1, 2]. He maintained that many tangled difficulties in understanding the Mishnah do not stem from the depth of the halakhic topic, but from errors of copyists and printers that crept into the text of the Mishnah over the generations [cite: 1, 2]. In order to clarify the original text, he systematically compared early printed editions of the Mishnah (such as the Naples edition and the Venice edition), the versions of the Mishnah as reflected in the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds, and ancient Eastern and Yemenite manuscripts [cite: 2, 3, 4, 6, 7]. Wherever he found a version that resolved the linguistic or halakhic difficulty, he decided in its favor and explained why the text accepted in the printed editions is mistaken [cite: 1, 2].
Second, Adani relied on autograph manuscripts and rare primary sources [cite: 7, 8]. An exceptional achievement in his method was his use of a rare manuscript of the Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah that arrived from the city of Aram Tzova (Aleppo in Syria), which was signed by the hand of the Rambam himself [cite: 8]. Adani notes several times in his commentary that he was puzzled by versions common in the printed editions, until he discovered from a corrected book written from the Rambam's own manuscript that the original version was entirely different [cite: 8]. The ability to examine the Rambam's words from his original manuscript enabled him to restore to their former state many interpretations that had been confused in the accepted translations [cite: 8].
Third, Adani incorporated into his commentary linguistic, grammatical and realia-based analysis [cite: 2, 6, 7]. He was careful to clarify the words of the Mishnah precisely, relying extensively on the book "HaAruch" by Rabbi Natan of Rome and on analysis of linguistic roots in Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic [cite: 6]. In addition, he showed great interest in the realia of Mishnaic times, such as the structure of the Temple, geography, earthenware and vegetation [cite: 7]. In the manuscript of his commentary on tractate Middot he even incorporated detailed geometric drawings of the plan of the Temple and the Temple Mount [cite: 7].
Fourth, the commentary offers a broad interpretive synthesis and halakhic ruling [cite: 1, 2]. Adani is not satisfied with local explanation, but brings in order the commentaries of Rashi, the Rambam, the Rosh, Rabbeinu Shimshon of Sens (the Rash), the Rav (Rabbi Ovadia of Bartenura), the Nimukei Yosef, and the glosses of Rabbi Yehosef Ashkenazi [cite: 6, 12]. He then traces the development of the topic in the Talmud and concludes with indications of the practical halakhic ruling in the Rambam and the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 2].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Influence and Legacy for Generations
Despite the enormous importance of "Melekhet Shlomo," the work was fated to remain in manuscript for about 250 years after the author's death [cite: 13, 14, 15]. This fate stemmed mainly from the precarious economic and political situation of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel in the 17th century, and the lack of resources to print a work of such enormous scope [cite: 1, 10].
Nevertheless, the manuscript was not lost and its influence began to seep through indirect channels [cite: 4]. The scholar Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel used Adani's glosses and versions when he published his edition of the Mishnayot in Amsterdam in 5392 (1632) [cite: 4]. In the 18th century, Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai (the Chida) saw Adani's manuscripts during his travels, praised them greatly and even quoted from them in his books [cite: 1, 4].
The great turning point in the dissemination of Adani's teaching occurred in the late 19th century, when the printers of the Romm Press (the Widow and Brothers Romm) in Vilna obtained the original manuscript (the autograph) of Rabbi Shlomo Adani [cite: 12]. In 5647 (1887), as part of the printing of their famous edition of the Mishnayot, they incorporated the "Melekhet Shlomo" commentary at the bottom of the page [cite: 12]. The editors of the Romm Press adopted a strict editorial policy: since Adani had copied in his commentary long passages from the "Tosafot Yom Tov" or from the "Nimukei Yosef," the editors omitted these passages in order to prevent duplication on the printed page, and left mainly his original novellae, his textual clarifications and his linguistic comments [cite: 12]. The printing of "Melekhet Shlomo" in the Vilna edition paved the way for recognition of his genius throughout the Jewish world [cite: 2, 12].
In the 20th century "Melekhet Shlomo" became a respected focus of academic research in the field of the language of the Sages and Mishnah textual criticism [cite: 3, 11]. Modern scholars, among them E. Z. Melamed, Y. N. Epstein, Y. Z. Feintuch and Yehuda Ratzaby, devoted comprehensive studies to analyzing Adani's sources and textual method [cite: 3, 7, 11]. Epstein showed in his book "Introduction to the Text of the Mishnah" that Adani's versions preserve ancient Eretz Israel and Eastern traditions of high fidelity to the source [cite: 7], while Feintuch surveyed his contribution to the reconstruction of Talmudic textual traditions [cite: 3, 11].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
The work of Rabbi Shlomo Adani, author of "Melekhet Shlomo," constitutes one of the peaks of Mishnah commentary of all generations [cite: 1, 2]. Out of a life reality saturated with grief, poverty and bereavement, he managed to produce a towering Torah-scholarly enterprise, characterized by textual precision, interpretive integrity and comprehensive mastery of the writings of the ancients [cite: 1, 2, 8, 10]. His commentary "Melekhet Shlomo" is not only an explanation of the Mishnah but a rare textual archive preserving manuscripts, lost versions and glosses of the great Rishonim and Acharonim [cite: 7, 8]. Its becoming an integral part of the standard editions of the Mishnah fixed its place as a permanent asset in the Jewish library, and as a foremost guide for every learner and researcher seeking to reach the depth of the Oral Torah [cite: 2, 12].
